idiom_name: handle exchange behind an explicit no-fail swap protocol
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: keep the state that must change together behind one replaceable handle (a pointer to a body, an index into a store, or a single reference to an immutable state object), then define the exchange as "temporary = a's handle; a's handle = b's handle; b's handle = temporary". The exchange must run no user code that can fail - no allocation, no copy of the represented resources, no locking, no callbacks - so it cannot report an error; the fallible steps (building the new state, validating it, acquiring resources) happen before the exchange and never inside it. Make the operation discoverable through the language's own swap protocol (ADL plus std::swap and the Swappable requirement in C++; multiple assignment, destructuring or a standard-library swap where the language provides one) so generic code uses the cheap version automatically instead of a copy-based default. Where the language has no swap protocol, a plain swap function on the handle plus the discipline "build first, exchange last" gives the same commit semantics.
code_sketch:
type T:                        # value whose state lives behind one handle
    state: Handle              # pointer / index / reference to the body

swap(a: T, b: T):              # must not allocate, lock or call user code
    t = a.state
    a.state = b.state
    b.state = t                # infallible commit

update(t: T, make_new_state):  # fallible work first, exchange last
    fresh = make_new_state(t.state)              # may fail - t unchanged
    t.state, fresh.state = fresh.state, t.state  # cannot fail
pitfalls: If the exchange touches anything that can fail (allocation, a lock, a callback, another object's copy), it is not the pattern: the caller's rollback path can now fail halfway and leave both objects inconsistent.
State that is not inside the exchanged handle (caches, observer lists, ownership back-pointers, mutexes) survives the exchange and silently describes the wrong body.

Swapping handles does not move external aliases: pointers, iterators and observers into the old body keep their target, which is intended sharing behaviour in copy-on-write and a bug in a value type that is supposed to be updated in place.
Self-swap and aliased handles must remain valid no-ops; a helper that assumes two distinct bodies can corrupt state when called with the same object twice.

Wrong move: call only qualified std::swap -> the namespace-level ADL overload can be bypassed and the generic move/copy path may be selected -> instead use using std::swap; swap(a, b) in generic code and provide the type's ADL swap.

Wrong move: mark a composite swap noexcept without checking every member or allocator -> a violated guarantee calls std::terminate instead of preserving a recoverable failure -> instead use conditional noexcept and is_nothrow_swappable checks, or make every exchanged handle genuinely non-throwing.

Wrong move: assume std::vector::swap is unconditionally noexcept -> allocator propagation/equality preconditions can invalidate that promise -> instead honor allocator traits and test the concrete type's nothrow-swappability before relying on it.
